title: Solitary Confinement: Cruel and Unusual
summary: Josh and Chuck examine solitary confinement in the United States and worldwide: what it is, how it differs from disciplinary and administrative segregation, its origins in Quaker-inspired penitentiary reform at Walnut Street Jail and Eastern State Penitentiary, the 1983 Marion Federal Prison lockdown that gave rise to supermax prisons, documented mental and physical harms, reduced-isolation reforms in England, the UN special rapporteur's report, the disputed Colorado study, and the Angola Three case including Albert Woodfox's 43-year isolation. The episode ends with listener mail correcting earlier episodes and covering Australian slang. An opening note promotes podcast month (TryPod).
topics: Eighth Amendment cruel and unusual punishment
Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: TryPod promotion
segments.summary: Hosts encourage listeners to share favorite podcasts during podcast month, using the TryPod hashtag.

segments.title: Opening banter and framing
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode as a follow-up to earlier prison coverage, frame solitary confinement as cruel and controversial, and describe typical conditions of 23 to 24 hours a day in small cells.

segments.title: Types of segregation and examples
segments.summary: Hosts distinguish disciplinary segregation from administrative segregation and pretrial holding, and discuss the case of Kalief Browder, held at Rikers Island for years, including in solitary, without conviction.

segments.title: Mentally ill in solitary and lack of oversight
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how mentally ill prisoners are often housed in solitary after deinstitutionalization, the lack of data and access for researchers, and the absence of judicial oversight over solitary placement.

segments.title: Quaker origins and early penitentiaries
segments.summary: The hosts trace solitary to Quaker ideas of penance at the Walnut Street Jail in Philadelphia in the late eighteenth century, and the abandonment of lockdown at Eastern State Penitentiary in 1829 after it caused social dysfunction and suicides.

segments.title: Marion lockdown and rise of supermax prisons
segments.summary: After two guards were killed at Marion Federal Prison in Illinois on October 22, 1983, the warden imposed a long lockdown that evolved into supermax prisons. The hosts connect the spread of supermax to the 1994 crime bill and mass incarceration in the US.

segments.title: Arguments for solitary and documented harms
segments.summary: Proponents cite deterrence, protection of inmates, control of escape risks, and punishment within prison. Hosts then review studies of harms including depression, hallucinations, sleep disruption, self-harm, suicide, and higher reoffending after release from supermax.

segments.title: Costs and international reform
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the higher cost of housing inmates in solitary or supermax, then England's reduction of long-term isolation in the 1980s through unit-based incentive systems, and recent restrictions on solitary for juveniles and the mentally ill in several states and federal prisons.

segments.title: UN report and Colorado study
segments.summary: Hosts describe UN special rapporteur Juan Mendez's report calling for reform and a Colorado Department of Corrections-funded study claiming inmate mental health can improve in solitary, which critics dispute.

segments.title: David Simon and private prisons
segments.summary: Hosts mention David Simon's advocacy against solitary and for-profit prisons and suggest a future episode on private prisons.

segments.title: Angola Three case
segments.summary: The hosts recount the Angola Three, Albert Woodfox, Herman Wallace and Robert King, held at Angola after a Black Panther chapter and prison activism. Woodfox spent about 43 years in isolation, the case rested on disputed evidence and witness Hezekiah Brown, Wallace was freed and died shortly after, and Woodfox was released in 2016. The hosts close by arguing that solitary conflicts with rehabilitation and that the Eighth Amendment has not been settled on it.
